set1.q: A 34-year-old woman has visible, dilated, tortuous veins of the thigh and calf that are tender to palpation, with aching heaviness after prolonged standing. Which is the most common predisposing factor for her condition?
opts: Recent pregnancy
Women are at higher risk after pregnancy, and it is a recognized risk factor. Family history remains the most common predisposing factor for varicose veins.
Regular heavy lifting
Heavy lifting produces periods of high venous pressure and adds risk. It is less common than family history, the leading predisposing factor for this condition.
Family history of varicose veins
Correct. The most common predisposing factor for varicose veins is family history, so ask whether relatives have them, and how old they were when they developed.
Prolonged standing at work
Long periods of standing raise venous pressure and are a recognized risk factor. It is not the most common predisposing factor, which is family history.

set1.q: A 38-year-old woman has long-standing swelling of both legs just above the ankles that is symmetric, with normal skin color and no ulcers or varicose veins. Cardiac, kidney and liver evaluations are normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Lymphedema
Lymphedema presents with unilateral swelling, no varicosities and pitting edema. Symmetric bilateral swelling just above the ankles in a woman describes lipedema.
Heart failure edema
Heart failure also swells both legs but comes with cardiac findings, and her cardiac, kidney and liver evaluations are normal. Symmetric swelling above the ankles is lipedema.
Lipedema

Correct. Bilateral, symmetric swelling just above the ankles in a woman, with normal cardiac, kidney and liver evaluations and no venous skin changes, is the description of lipedema in the differential of leg edema.
Chronic venous insufficiency
Insufficiency brings pitting edema with brown pigmentation, dermatitis or ulcers from venous hypertension. Her skin is normal and there are no varicose veins, so lipedema fits better.

set1.q: A 47-year-old woman has a tender, red, firm segment along a forearm vein after a peripheral intravenous catheter was removed. Venous duplex ultrasound shows a superficial vein with a thickened wall. Which additional finding would establish thrombophlebitis rather than phlebitis alone?
opts: Clot within the vein lumen

Correct. Wall thickening alone is phlebitis, inflammation of the vein wall without thrombus. Thickening together with clot in the lumen is thrombophlebitis, and the distinction matters because treatment differs.
Thickening of the vein wall
Wall thickening is already present and is common to both phlebitis and thrombophlebitis. Only clot within the lumen turns the picture into thrombophlebitis.
Reflux through incompetent valves
Valve reflux belongs to chronic venous disease such as varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency. It says nothing about clot inside an inflamed superficial vein.
Fluid collection around the vein
A perivenous fluid collection would raise concern for abscess or infection around the vein. Thrombophlebitis is defined by clot within the lumen of the thickened vein.
